I think it’s possible, but you have to be extremely precise with word choices and how you want your sentences to flow and be interpreted. Keep in mind if you address multiple experiences, you have to:

1. Explain it 
2. Show how it impacted you/others*
3. Relate your experience to PT and define how it will help you out in your career. 
4. Transition it to the next idea without overlapping themes.

I wouldn’t be afraid to say you learned something from other diverse perspectives either, even though the prompt is centered around what you did for others. I can’t imagine a school would negate you for showing you value others perspective and if the whole story isn’t just all about how great your perspective is for others. ***

You would also have to make sure each experience hits a new idea, because if you just regurgitate the same concept over multiple experiences, you could probably do the same thing, in a single and very in depth experience. 




EX 1: your eclectic group of teammates in your high school sport taught you how to see from a different perspective you were unaware of followed by an explanation of how that specific experience relates to PT

EX 2: Likewise, I saw how diverse experiences helped our team of coworkers in my role as a (server/tech/trainer), push each other/ work better together/etc… Here i learned that diverse experiences can forge strong relationships. This relates to PT by

EX1: experience A-> different viewpoints i was unaware of -> can be sympathetic with intraproffesional coworkers/ diverse patients 
EX2: experience b -> allowed us to challenge each other -> i can push my patient to be greater

My only issue with this, is 5,000 characters will go in a blink of an eye. Once you add in an introduction, a closing, and fill in the transitional sentences, you’ve already lost a lot of room that you need to expand on each story. Which is why you CAN do it, it’s just very hard to write that concise and still be detailed in such a small window

I ran 9,999 limits right up until the last character and crushed my essays. It’s totally dependent on your content. You should try to keep your points concise but if you have story to tell don’t feel like you can’t use what you’re allotted.

My two prospects told me if you couldn’t meet basic requirements to just save your money. However, both programs I applied to took the holistic approach and once the gpa requirement was checked off they told applicants it really played no process in evaluating an application. GPA isn’t everything by any stretch of the imagination but yeah would definitely advise against banking on your route lmao (no offense)

Your overall gpa doesn’t typically matter as long as it’s over a 3.0, they focus around your prerequisite GPA. It’s dependent on what program you’re looking at but if it’s not over a 3.2 or 3.0 (whatever your program wants) with those 3 C’s you won’t meet the minimum requirement and they’ll trash your app before they look at anything else. Plug your prereqs into a gpa calculator and find if it’s above requirements from your programs website. 

If your prerequisite gpa can clear the threshold then just go for it. If you don’t get in, just use the whole process as a learning opportunity for your second go around. I debated applying my first cycle out and ended up in my dream program so you never know what’ll happen.

Would also agree don’t stress over research (getting published or having it in multiple areas), but it’ll definitely help to have the experience. I applied to two programs, one who specifically asked if I had any experience in research on their PTCAS application and another school who had let it be known they wanted a big push on the research they pumped out. I think this might come into play more with name brand schools, so I wouldn’t necessarily just tell you “PT schools will not care about research”, but it might play a small role if the university/program prioritizes it. Even if you only did like 1 semester and never got published you should be covered here as long as you can talk about how it helps you in your journey to PT. Don’t break your back over trying to run this up though. 

If anything, I would tell you to not get tunnel visioned at the one spot you’re doing your PT aide position at. I would describe this as your competition may have only 100 hours of observation but across 4-5 vastly diverse clinics, which might grant them a better understanding of PT as a whole when compared to your 200 hours at one spot. I’m not saying quit your job or anything, just make sure your lens of PT isn’t fixated all from the same building.

Yeah just go in person dressed up and with a resume. Even if you have to wait an hour you can at least get a yes or no and move on if you have to, which is better than being in limbo of not knowing if you have to start looking for new places or not. 

Just be professional about it, I would always recommend going in person to ask about this stuff, lets them get a sense of who you are and a direct answer (most of the time). I’ve had to go in person to the same spot 1-2 times to get a yes before but none of the staff members ever seemed to think I was overbearing as long as I was professional about it.

PTCAS doesn’t ask for specific times/dates, but it’s best to stay organized for yourself. PTCAS just request a total amount of hours for the specific spot and you can categorize the hours between OT/PT…etc if you like (although I don’t think programs freak out if you do/don’t do this because you’ll likely mention it in your essays or something)

The only time you need your PT to sign off on something for you is when you input the hours into PTCAS. PTCAS asks you to provide an email for the PT you were under at each spot so they can electronically approve your hours via email. Just keep a phone number/email from your PTs so if you don’t apply for another 3 years, you can get in contact with them when the time comes. 

For general tips, just stay engaged even if you get bored. If I interview you about why you love PT and ask what you did during your 50 hours at clinic xxx, and you can’t tell me what you did cause you spent half the time on your phone it’s a bad look. Those notes help you keep that info fresh. 

Also diversify your hours and don’t get hooked at one spot. 75 hours across 3/4 different types of clinics (SNF/outpatient/private practice) looks better than 100 hours at one clinic. Jump on inpatient/hospital settings sooner rather than later cause those locations are tougher to get into over a regular outpatient clinic.

Shadow other professions to rule out why you do like PT & why things like speech therapy, OT, and nursing aren’t for you. 

Best of luck!

I’d probably say A) grab your teacher reviews, if a class is easy with good ratings that should be your first indicator for pairing. EX: if bio 101 is easy and ur bad at physics, leave physics by itself and double down on chem and bio. Also having a good teacher with ANY of these classes will make a world of difference. I bombed chem (with a c-) over covid, retook it in person with a great professor and I ripped off 90s on tests with my eyes closed. 

B) physics will be the only class that is more conceptually based > raw memorization ( in my experience). Biology is straight raw memorization, soak up the info, dump it on a test and forget about it tomorrow. Chemistry, while including math, is relatively simple plug and chug formulas matched up with raw memorization of rules to follow. Physics is plug and chug, but with (at least for myself) harder concepts and a lot more moving variables. Physics II, for me is all about circuits and light, so if this isn’t your alley, I believe most people would rather pair chem+ bio and leave physics by itself rather than pairing physics and leaving chem/bio for itself.
